clue.text: Ask for amount of electricity

blocks.note: first meaning: to ask a price for goods or a service
second meaning: the quantity of electricity stored in a battery or carried by a particle

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a utility bill demanding payment for power used; the two halves are separate senses of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb names setting a price for something, and the noun is the physics term for stored electrical energy in a battery.

clue.text: Price on grotty old sheep’s cheese

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A shopper balks at the price tag on a tired-looking old wedge of cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grotty' seems to describe the cheese, but it is the signal to rearrange; 'old' adds the extra letter, grotty being British slang for nasty or shabby.
explanation.definitionFit: Pecorino is an Italian hard cheese made from ewe's milk, its name coming from the Italian word pecora for a ewe.

clue.text: Film lost in hurricane?

second meaning, read literally: something carried off and lost when a great storm blows

explanation.definitionFit: The title names a classic Hollywood picture, and the same words literally describe belongings swept off by violent gales.

clue.text: Dismiss bank worker

second meaning: the person who pays out and takes in money at a counter

explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to discharge from service dishonourably; as a noun it is the teller handling cash at a counter.

clue.text: Astronomy in part confusing, take what help you can get!

definitions.text: take what help you can get!

indicators.note: something confusing is jumbled and muddled, so the preceding letters must be sorted into a new order

explanation.walkthrough: 'In part' looks like a qualifier meaning 'partly', but both words are letters to rearrange along with the science.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says that in a crisis any refuge will do, so you accept whatever assistance is offered.

clue.text: Have a go at munching a starter of Irish sausage

explanation.walkthrough: 'Have a go at' looks like 'try', but it is the British idiom for attacking someone verbally.
explanation.definitionFit: Salami is a cured, spiced Italian sausage, usually served sliced cold, so the general term covers it.

clue.text: Singer dismissing case of English composer

explanation.walkthrough: William Walton was a twentieth-century English composer; strip his outer letters to leave the voice part.
explanation.definitionFit: An alto is a vocalist with the lowest female or highest adult male voice range, so a kind of singer.

clue.text: Footwear on your bike, did you say?

explanation.surface: A cyclist is asked whether a boot or trainer belongs on their bicycle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On your bike' looks like it is about cycling, but it is British slang for 'clear off', which is the meaning of the dismissive 'shoo'.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoe is the standard item worn on the foot, the most common kind of footwear people buy and wear.

clue.text: Female cells in Govan neither opening nor closing

explanation.surface: Prison cells for women in a Glasgow district have doors that neither open nor shut.
explanation.walkthrough: Govan is a district of Glasgow; 'cells' looks like prison cells, but these are biological ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Ova are egg cells, the female reproductive cells produced by the ovaries of animals and humans.

clue.text: Nobleman coming in to New York, not far off

an earl is a British nobleman

explanation.surface: An aristocrat's transatlantic arrival at New York is close at hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not far off' seems to describe the arrival in time or distance, but it is the definition, meaning 'almost'.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something is almost the case means it is close to being so, the same idea as only a short distance short.

clue.text: Poet skint, zero pocketed

indicators.note: a pocket holds something inside it, so one piece is tucked within another

blocks.note: skint is British slang for having no money
zero looks like the letter O

explanation.walkthrough: Rupert Brooke was the English poet of 'The Soldier'; skint is British slang for penniless.
explanation.definitionFit: Rupert Brooke was an English poet best known for his First World War sonnets, so the surname names a poet.

clue.text: Figure crack in the pan fixed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' looks like a break in the pan, but it means an attempt; 'figure' is a geometric shape, not a number or a person.
explanation.definitionFit: A heptagon is a plane shape with seven straight sides, and geometry calls any such shape a figure.

clue.text: The ground ain’t electrified

explanation.definitionFit: Grammar calls the word 'the' the definite article, as opposed to the indefinite 'a' or 'an'.

explanation.definitionFit: To lap is to drink with the tongue, as a cat or dog takes up milk or water from a bowl.

clue.text: Tap out wrong letters in slightly obscure exercise

explanation.walkthrough: 'Letters' suggests post or a letter-selection device, but here it means characters typed on a keyboard.
explanation.definitionFit: To mistype is to hit the wrong keys when typing, producing errors in the text you key in.

clue.text: A part mixed with wet, running liquid

explanation.definitionFit: Tap water is the supply that flows from household faucets, the familiar running water of a home.

clue.text: Look inside trophy for shell

explanation.definitionFit: A scallop is a bivalve mollusc with a fan-shaped ribbed shell, and the word also names that shell.

clue.text: Fast, as crowd on feet?

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means at great speed, as in running to catch a train, so it matches the adverb sense of quickly.

clue.text: Whole testament I put in before

explanation.definitionFit: Entire and whole are synonyms describing something complete, with no part missing or left out.

clue.text: Fairly sure thing!

clue.text: Wisest hunter hosts a presentation
